title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s buses: a blueprint for governing Britain | Editorial
content: The prime minister is right to think that taking Manchester’s model national could widen opportunity, clean the air and rebuild state capacity. Other public services could be next Barely a month into his premiership, Andy Burnham is already taking the lessons of Manchester’s buses national. This week his government backed the West Midlands mayor Richard Parker’s move to bring the region’s main bus operation into public control. In July, he announced that he would reinstate a £2 national bus fare cap from January 2027. He’s also expanding free bus travel for disabled people to all hours. Transport affordability is clearly part of Mr Burnham’s cost of living programme. That is to be applauded, as is the emphasis on public transport, which – importantly for Labour – reduces social exclusion, boosts local economies, and is better for the environment. Yet buses may matter to Mr Burnham for another reason: they offer a blueprint for how he wants to govern. This is because Mr Burnham seems to have a worked-out model. He told the Times this week that the prescription for services such as water, housing and energy isn’t yet clear, “with the exception of buses”. Public control, Mr Burnham reasons, gives government the power to make provision cheaper and more reliable – and to shape it around the public interest. For buses, that means the government determining the shape of the network even where private companies run the services. Municipal ownership this is not. Despite that, more money will be needed. Austerity slashed public transport budgets, and consequently bus journeys fell. Outside London, buses clock up about 736m miles a year, nearly a third below 2005. Getting back to a decent service would cost a paltry sum. For £300m a year, England could get buses back into its worst-served communities. For about £1bn, the Campaign for Better Transport calculated, ministers could provide decent, frequent services in towns and rural areas. In 2021, the Campaign to Protect Rural England put the price of a Swiss-style bus network – an hourly service from 6am to midnight for every village of more than 300 people – at £2.7bn a year. Accounting for inflation, that would be £3.4bn today, just 1.5% of the NHS budget. Public transport isn’t only about moving people around. London’s extensive tube, rail and bus network gave Sir Sadiq Khan the room to introduce Ulez. The scheme charged drivers of older, more polluting vehicles and brought measurable health benefits. A study has shown that children’s lungs grew bigger and stronger after Ulez was introduced. It is worth noting that Mr Burnham abandoned Manchester’s clean-air charging zone when the post-pandemic cost of replacing dirty vehicles threatened to fall heavily on businesses. He instead pressed ahead with the Bee Network, giving Manchester a more affordable public-transport alternative, while simultaneously spending public money cleaning up the city’s bus fleet. It was a politically shrewd sequence: improve the alternative so that you could persuade people to use their cars less. Both Theresa May and Sir John Major have tried to diminish Mr Burnham’s mayoral experience by contrasting “running Manchester” and “dealing with buses” with being in Downing Street. Yet the prime minister appears to regard buses not as an incidental part of his record but as an exemplar for his government. The Centre for Cities thinktank argues that poor transport makes big English urban centres outside London effectively smaller in economic terms, by cutting workers off from opportunities. Perhaps his critics have it backwards: buses are not a distraction from governing Britain; connecting people to cities is part of the job.
centralIdea: The editorial highlights how bringing bus services under public control, modeled after Manchester's system, serves as a practical blueprint for national governance to improve public services, boost local economies, and address environmental concerns.
skimming: The UK government is backing regional moves to bring bus operations back under public control, inspired by Manchester's successful model.
Public control allows the state to regulate fares and routes, offering a template for managing other public utilities like water and energy.
Revitalizing the national bus network requires a relatively small financial investment compared to other major public sectors like the NHS.

This is a crucial punctuation rule tested in CAT sentence correction.

title: The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status | Editorial
content: Scientific specimens are being sold to foreign museums or snapped up by the super-rich. They should have the same legal protections as works of art As Sir David Attenborough has observed, “there’s nothing more magical than finding a shiny shell and knowing you’re the first person to have seen it for 150 million years”. Senior museum figures are campaigning for fossils to be classed as national treasures, according to the Waverley criteria, which control the export of objects considered culturally important to the nation. But the rules only cover natural treasures that are “made”, excluding fossils. These calls come after a private collection from the Jurassic Coast was sold to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi for a reported eight-figure sum. Both the Natural History Museum in London and Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) were offered the 318 fossils, but they didn’t have the funds. Unlike countries such as Brazil and Mongolia, where fossils belong to the state, Britain relies largely on a voluntary code of conduct. The line between fossils as scientific specimens and fossils as aesthetic objects is becoming increasingly blurred – and their value is rocketing accordingly. Where once Damien Hirst’s shark made waves on the contemporary art scene, a dinosaur fossil appeared at London’s Frieze Masters in 2023. Last month, a 67m-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex fossil called Gus broke records at a Sotheby’s auction in New York. He toppled Apex, a stegosaurus bought by an American hedge fund manager in 2024, now on loan to the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and Stan, another T rex, was also acquired by the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in 2022. Big beasts of Hollywood have also got in on the act, with Nicolas Cage and Leonardo DiCaprio battling it out for a fossil. Today’s dinomania has everyone from tech giants to TikTokers in its grip. But there is nothing new about fossil collecting. Mary Anning, a cabinetmaker’s daughter born in Lyme Regis in 1799, was one the UK’s greatest palaeontologists, although, as a woman, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London. Her life story inspired Tracy Chevalier’s 2009 novel Remarkable Creatures and the 2020 film Ammonite. The Victorian passion for palaeontology provides the backdrop to the clandestine love stories in John Fowles’s French Lieutenant’s Woman (also set in Lyme Regis) and AS Byatt’s Possession. Fossils have provided a rich seam for writers and film‑makers from Tennyson (an enthusiastic collector on the Isle of Wight) to Noel Streatfeild’s 1936 children’s classic Ballet Shoes starring the foundling Fossil sisters, to Steven Spielberg’s Jurassic Park blockbusters. Last year’s Jurassic World Reborn has been credited with contributing to the recent collecting boom. Fossils and dinosaurs are a source of childhood wonder. These long-dead specimens speak to us across millions of years. But they also hold important clues to the future, recording changing ecosystems, climate and biodiversity, providing vital evidence in the environmental emergency. Without private hunters, many of these discoveries would not be made, especially in rapidly eroding landscapes like the Jurassic Coast. These collections are better in a museum, even if it is abroad. And the UK has no shortage of fossils from other countries. But measures to protect them are overdue. Important fossils should not be allowed to disappear into the collections of the super-rich. They should be accessible for scientists to study and the public to enjoy for hundreds of years to come. They are national treasures and deserve to be treated as such.
centralIdea: The editorial argues that fossils found in the UK should be granted national treasure status and legal export protections similar to works of art, preventing important scientific specimens from being monopolized by wealthy private buyers and ensuring they remain accessible to the public and researchers.
skimming: Museum figures in the UK are campaigning to classify fossils as national treasures under the Waverley criteria to restrict their export.
Unlike countries where fossils are state property, the UK relies on a voluntary code, allowing rare specimens to be sold to wealthy private collectors or foreign museums.
The commercial value of fossils is skyrocketing due to growing interest from celebrities and the super-rich, blurring the line between science and art.
While private collectors aid in fossil discovery, stronger regulations are essential to preserve these vital clues to Earth's history for public and scientific benefit.

title: The Guardian view on GCSE results: much to celebrate, much to reform | Editorial
content: Another post-pandemic cohort has shown its resilience and talent. But growing inequalities of outcome must be addressed Most pupils who received their GCSE results this week were in the penultimate year of primary school when Covid struck, disrupting their preparation for secondary education. As with other post-pandemic cohorts, their achievements are therefore a testament to their ability, resilience and determination. A strong set of results, particularly in the core subjects of English and maths, should also be seen as a tribute to teachers dealing with ever expanding workloads. Overall the impression is one of a welcome return to stability, as the legacy of the years of cancelled exams and teacher assessments is left behind. The proportion of top grades awarded in England, Wales and Northern Ireland rose compared with last year, but only by a tenth of a percentage point, while the overall pass rate fell by the same margin to 67.3% – the same as in 2019. Nevertheless, the latest results throw up familiar grounds for concern. The ongoing decline in language learning appears to be accelerating to an alarming degree, with GCSE take-up in French and other modern languages falling sharply again. A culturally enriching part of the curriculum is in danger of becoming the preserve of affluent state schools and the independent sector. More broadly, inequalities of outcome suggest a fundamental change in approach is required to address regional disparities that have become entrenched. London schools once again pulled away from those in the north and the Midlands when it came to the awarding of top grades. Recent research has shown that good GCSE grades have a disproportionately beneficial impact on the life chances of pupils from less privileged backgrounds. A levelling up strategy is urgently needed. While overall results in English and maths were impressive, a significant proportion of teenagers failed to achieve a grade 4 pass. The data also confirmed that the policy in England of imposing compulsory resits in those subjects is blighting lives rather than raising standards. Only 18.8% of those aged 17 and over achieved the requisite pass grade in English, down from last year, with an even smaller proportion achieving a grade 4 in maths. Far too many young people are becoming trapped in a demoralising and humiliating cycle of failure, which is blocking their progress into the world of work. The government plans to introduce a new “stepping stone” qualification to build confidence ahead of resits, but a more radical overhaul is needed. At a time when an estimated 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training, developing a more nuanced approach, including alternative pathways, should be a priority. An overhaul is what Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell, are promising. From 2028, the educational landscape in England may change significantly for 14- to 16-year-olds. The prime minister appears committed to rebalancing the curriculum by expanding the number of technical education options available to students, in a reprise of his approach as the mayor of Greater Manchester. If a true parity of esteem is to be established between academic and vocational routes, as Mr Burnham desires, it will require a significant injection of resources. But the focus is the right one. Though there was much to celebrate as another post-Covid cohort came of age, the inequalities and failures revealed again by this year’s results are long overdue for attention. title: The Guardian view on Trump’s MMR executive order: endangering the children he claims to care about | Editorial
content: The president’s empty advice that children should receive separate jabs against measles, mumps and rubella will only lead to less take-up by parents Nobody wants to hurt a child. The howl of pain, the tears, the look of betrayed shock all make it very hard to deliver a cherished small person to the needle-wielding nurse. But that’s part of being a responsible parent. It becomes a lot tougher if mum or dad is being fed mixed and erroneous messages about the benefits and harms of vaccination. Parents have to make a lot of decisions about what’s right for their child, from the school they should go to and the food they should eat to the hours they should spend on the phone or watching TV. In the US, Donald Trump wants them to add another: do they choose to give their children separate jabs against measles, mumps and rubella, involving six visits to the clinic, or should they opt for the combined MMR vaccine, which does the job in two? For decades, the vast majority of families have been taking the advice of doctors, accepting their assurance that the MMR vaccine is safe and very effective. But what are they to think when a US president announces that the triple jab could be “quite lethal” and signs an executive order advising states to offer separate vaccines? For the moment, what Mr Trump is proposing is an empty choice. The individual vaccines are not available. They have not been widely used in decades. In the US and in the UK, they don’t have a licence, and to get one, pharma companies such as GSK and Merck & Co would probably have to run new clinical trials to prove that they work and are safe, which would take years. Both have already said that no published scientific evidence supports splitting the MMR vaccine into single shots. They are not rushing to invest in making them, for all the US president’s enthusiasm. But we are likely to see a rerun of the furore and distress in 1998 caused by Andrew Wakefield, the British gastroenterologist (not an infectious diseases specialist) who declared that the MMR vaccine was linked to the gut disorder Crohn’s disease and thence to autism. His evidence-free advice was for parents to seek separate vaccines. As now, they were not readily available, so many children went without. Measles vaccination levels dropped alarmingly and measles cases rose. Struck off as a doctor, Mr Wakefield now lives in Texas, hero-worshipped by vaccine sceptics, and his views are embraced by all those suspicious of or hostile to the medical and scientific establishment, including the president and his health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. They fit an anti-science agenda that has recently seen the pursuit by a congressional committee of Dr Anthony Fauci, who led the US response to Covid-19 and is now being accused of covering up its origins. Mr Trump and RFK Jr already aim to shrink the vaccine schedule in the US from 18 to 11 shots, citing Denmark, where fewer vaccines are given to young children. But Denmark offers universal high-quality healthcare and excellent screening programmes to pick up those at risk. The US does not, and children fall through the cracks. No other country recommends single measles, mumps and rubella vaccines. But such is the confusion that some parents are likely to take away the message that the combined jab is unsafe – and that no jab is a better choice. President Trump is putting at risk the very “beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children” that he claims to care about. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid matters | Editorial
content: The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries For months health experts have warned that the scale of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could surpass the one that swept west Africa in 2014-16. This week, the authorities in the DRC announced that a grim milestone has already been passed: at least 2,325 people have died from the virus, making it the deadliest of the country’s 17 outbreaks and the fastest-growing in history. There is no effective vaccine against Bundibugyo – a rare strain of the virus that spread fatally undetected during the spring, often being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. In contrast to neighbouring Uganda, which succeeded in eliminating an outbreak, multiple factors are combining to let the disease rip through the DRC. The worst-affected region is contested by armed groups, and a context of population displacement and chronic insecurity has made monitoring and surveillance more difficult. Ebola treatment centres have been attacked as a result of misinformation and community distrust. The impact of this dire set of circumstances has been disastrously compounded by choices made in the west and, above all, in the United States. International aid cuts have deprived the DRC of vital human and material resources with which to fight back. In 2014, as the scale of the Ebola crisis in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea became clear, Barack Obama addressed the United Nations general assembly and mobilised a global response that was crucial in containing the outbreak. The US Agency for International Development (USAID) led efforts to train local health workers, pursue contact tracing and implement an eventual vaccination programme. The contrast with the Trump administration is stark and shaming. Last year, as the de facto head of the now defunct “department of government efficiency”, Elon Musk was given licence to implement swingeing cuts that led to the eventual dismantling of USAID. In the DRC, the direct consequence was the weakening of local health infrastructure and surveillance capacities, leaving one of the poorest countries in the world still more vulnerable. Also lost was a wealth of institutional experience and expertise gained in combating emergencies such as the one now unfolding. The US has further undermined the capacity for coordinated international action by withdrawing from the World Health Organization, to which it had been one of the biggest donors. European countries, notably Britain, Germany and France, have also been viewing international aid as luxury expenditure and cutting back. Last year, Sir Keir Starmer announced that from 2027 UK aid would be reduced from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3%. Against such a backdrop, the lack of diplomatic urgency over the current crisis, compared with 2014, should not perhaps come as a surprise. But that does not make it any less disappointing. The Ebola outbreak in west Africa laid bare the risk of regional and global disruption as a result of inadequate health infrastructure. A thousand pieties were then uttered in the wake of the Covid pandemic regarding the need to invest in global health security and future preparedness. Subsequent actions by governments have belied those words, leaving the DRC exposed to an epidemic that is threatening to spiral out of control. Belatedly, the global community needs to mobilise to address the threat. More fundamentally, it needs to draw the right lessons from a case study in why international aid matters. title: The Guardian view on the Grenfell Tower fire: Britain is letting companies pass the buck | Editorial
content: Victims received less compensation than shareholders in the company behind its flammable cladding. Parliament must make corporations pay for harm caused There is something profoundly wrong when the company behind Grenfell Tower’s flammable cladding paid more compensation to its shareholders than to victims of the disaster. Of Arconic’s £86m in Grenfell-related settlements, all but £1.5m was covered by insurers. Hardly enough to make a multinational think again. The company whose product the inquiry found was the “primary cause” of the fire’s rapid spread has ended up paying only a fraction of the wider social cost, while the multibillion-pound bill for making hundreds of buildings safe falls largely on the state. In June 2017, 72 people – including 18 children – died in London’s Grenfell Tower fire. Almost a decade later, nobody has been criminally charged over its causes. It’s hard to conclude anything but that Britain’s system of corporate accountability is rotten. A new report by the thinktank Common Wealth and the financial investigations group FIND suggests putting right this state of affairs in England and Wales by adopting two changes that parliament could enact quickly. The first is a “failure to prevent” law that would make companies responsible for having adequate systems to prevent foreseeable serious harm. The second is to adopt a “punitive damages” approach. Rather than compensating victims for their loss, punitive damages ask what a company should pay for its conduct. Such an award against Arconic could have been used to meet the costs of remediation, the report says, “at no public cost”. This is possible in America. Some Grenfell families tried to bring a case under US law, where damages can punish and deter corporate wrongdoing, not just compensate victims. Currently, Meta is accused in a California court of intentionally addicting children to Facebook and Instagram in pursuit of profit. It denies wrongdoing, but says litigation potentially exposes it to $1.4tn in penalties and changes to its products. Whatever the eventual outcome, the case shows how alleged social harm can be a company-sized risk. Arconic successfully argued that the Grenfell families’ case be heard in British courts, where civil compensation and criminal punishment are kept separate. The Metropolitan police are investigating 57 individuals and 20 organisations as criminal suspects, but no charges are expected before Grenfell’s tenth anniversary. Compare that with Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court fire, which killed 168 people in November 2025. Authorities immediately treated it as a potential crime involving corporate actors. Within seven months, seven people and two firms faced manslaughter charges. No one is suggesting authoritarian Hong Kong as a model. But nearly a decade without charges in Britain, against seven months in the far east, is an uncomfortable contrast. There are reasons why justice has taken so long: the Covid pandemic disrupted the Grenfell public inquiry involving hundreds of core participants, and responsibility stretches across manufacturers, certifiers, architects, contractors and regulators. This exposes a deeper problem: the more entities involved, the easier it becomes for blame for a disaster to disappear between them. Lawmakers know how to stop companies passing the buck. The polluter pays in environmental law. There are recall obligations in product safety and collective redress in competition law. Why aren’t legal principles that are already used to force companies to account for economic and consumer harms being extended to catastrophic social harms? Until they are, the law will remain better at protecting investors rather than the public from corporate wrongdoing. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on global inequality: extreme wealth threatens democracy | Editorial
content: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani shows Britain’s Andy Burnham that confronting billionaires need not mean the end of cooperation with Donald Trump In November, Californians will vote on a one-off 5% levy on residents worth more than $1bn. The union-backed plan could raise $100bn, more than enough to replace federal healthcare funding stripped away by Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. About 200 very rich people would pay. But the referendum is becoming a test of whether extreme wealth can buy the political power to defeat a popular redistributive policy. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has already spent $100m backing opposition to the tax – a fraction of the $13bn bill he could face. Other billionaires are joining him. Whether voters can impose costs on the super-rich once their fortunes are big enough to shape the political process is now an open question. That alone should trouble any democracy. It’s a long way from Mr Brin’s west coast lair of Mountain View to Andy Burnham’s Makerfield constituency. But the prime minister should heed the call from prominent progressive academics – led by the Nobel prize winner Joseph Stiglitz – urging Britain to join a new global push to tackle inequality. Prof Stiglitz wants help creating a new UN International Panel on Inequality (IPI). This stems from the G20’s first-ever inequality report, which warned that the yawning gap between rich and poor was a human-made crisis corroding democracy and social cohesion while blocking efforts to tackle the climate emergency. The academics argue that Mr Burnham’s Makerfield test – which aims to be fairer to places neglected by Westminster – should apply abroad as well as at home. By connecting the government’s domestic programme to its foreign policy, a distinct Burnhamism could take shape. Between 2000 and 2024, the richest 1% captured 41% of new global wealth; the poorest half received 1%. Britain mirrors this divide. The economist Gabriel Zucman says the UK’s richest 0.001% – about 200 families – held wealth worth 5% of GDP in 1989. Today, those families command an astonishing 25% of the country’s GDP. When Mr Burnham travels to the UN next month, he should back the IPI and make tackling global inequality a priority of Britain’s 2027 G20 presidency. Prof Stiglitz argues that extreme inequality is a policy choice, turbocharged by financial deregulation, weaker labour protections and privatisation. Highly unequal countries are seven times more likely to suffer democratic backsliding or authoritarian drift. Taxing the ultra-wealthy should be part of Britain’s response to a worldwide emergency. After Labour’s aid cuts, Mr Burnham also needs a credible way of saying Britain is back in global development. The IPI gives him an inexpensive initiative around which to build reform of international taxation, debt relief and illicit financial flows. None of this suggests that the UK wants an unproductive relationship with Washington. The White House is threatening the UK over its plans for a digital services tax, with the US warning that Mr Trump’s threat of retaliatory 100% tariffs is real. Policy disagreement need not poison the relationship. Mr Trump has denounced Zohran Mamdani’s New York luxury second-home tax as a “dangerous political experiment” and threatened to block it. Yet despite clashing, the leftwing mayor and the rightwing president continue to talk, cooperating on housing and immigration cases. Their warm White House meeting in February suggests that Mr Trump may respect politicians who openly disagree with him more than those who bend over backwards not to offend him. Perhaps Mr Burnham should take heart: being true to himself may work.

title: The Guardian view on writers’ houses: a museum of one’s own | Editorial
content: The Wordsworth Trust has acquired a second home. Cherished authors including George Eliot don’t even have one Interest in all things Jane Austen remains high, following the celebrations of her 250th anniversary. In September, the museum based in her former home in Chawton, Hampshire, will host a Persuasion festival. But a less obvious beneficiary of this spike in interest is a museum dedicated to two writers she never met: William and Dorothy Wordsworth. The success of the BBC television series The Other Bennet Sister – which portrayed Mary, a minor character in Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, as a Wordsworth enthusiast – has led to an influx of visitors to Dove Cottage in Cumbria. This has been a big year for the Wordsworth Trust, which owns the cottage, owing to its purchase of another house: Rydal Mount, two miles to the east. When this building is reopened, the poet will become one of a handful of authors, along with Charles Dickens and Thomas Hardy, to have more than one of his homes opened to visitors. These can be extraordinarily evocative places, brought to life by knowledgable guides. The modest cottages occupied by Hardy and Coleridge before they were famous stand in stark contrast to the aristocratic grandeur of other National Trust houses – and are an important reminder of how ordinary people once lived. In homes such as Monk’s House in East Sussex, near where Virginia Woolf drowned in the River Ouse, and Keats House in Hampstead, where the poet became ill with tuberculosis, death casts unavoidable shadows. Rydal Mount was sold by its previous owners in part due to a drop in numbers, and curators must be adept in capitalising on any new sources of interest. At the Brontë Parsonage in Yorkshire, an exhibition accompanied this year’s release of a new Wuthering Heights film; at Anne Hathaway’s cottage in Stratford-upon-Avon, Hamnet tours are on offer. Turning their homes into museums is, of course, not the only way to commemorate writers in the built environment. Edinburgh’s main railway station, Waverley, is famously the only one in the world named after a novel; Walter Scott, who wrote it, also has a monument across the road. National portrait galleries in Edinburgh and London depict authors alongside artists, scientists, royals, politicians and others. Buildings across the UK are adorned with blue plaques; William Shakespeare has a statue in Leicester Square. No writer of colour has yet had their British home turned into a museum. Since this transformation generally happens years after an author’s death, this is not surprising; immigrants from India, the Caribbean and Africa, and their descendants, mostly made their mark on the world of books from the mid-20th century onwards. Hopefully more houses, or flats, will be opened in future; VS Naipaul’s book The Enigma of Arrival offers a vivid, semi-fictional account of his years in a borrowed cottage on a Wiltshire estate. George Eliot is a more perplexing absence from the map of homes to visit – all the more so since her novel Middlemarch recently topped two Guardian polls. While the London house that she shared with George Henry Lewes was demolished, and the Arbury Estate where she was born is currently closed, efforts to restore a building linked to her family near Nuneaton have so far not succeeded. But a replica of her sitting room is in the town’s museum, while Coventry’s Herbert Art Gallery has her piano and desk. Fundraisers should be encouraged to try again: the 150th anniversary of her death falls in 2030. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Jason Arday: a tragedy that demands reflection | Editorial
content: Legitimate scrutiny became entangled with a racial argument about merit and diversity. His death raises questions about how society treats black success and failure The tragic death of Jason Arday raises serious questions about race, institutional authority and what happens to people in a society increasingly organised around public reputation. Arday, who resigned earlier this month as a professor at the University of Cambridge, was found dead at his home last week. He was 41. His family and friends have lost somebody they loved and cared for. Arday had publicly said that the scrutiny of allegations concerning his academic work and claims he had made about his life was taking a profound toll. That he then died amid an intense and continuing media examination of his life is deeply troubling. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, was right to call this “a moment for reflection”. This does not mean suppressing difficult questions, ignoring why there remain a pitifully small number of black professors in British universities, or attacking legitimate journalism. But in a polarised world it should see the media ask how proper scrutiny can widen into something more encompassing; how race affects the meaning attached to an individual’s alleged failings; and whether separate valid stories can, via social media, have an overwhelming effect. In Arday’s case, alleged shortcomings in his record rapidly became weaponised by the right in an argument about diversity and black academic advancement. Arday’s story – an autistic child from a council estate who became a Cambridge professor aged just 37 – was remarkable. The university publicised the symbolic dimensions of his appointment as a young, black, neurodivergent man. He had been accused of plagiarism in his doctoral thesis – allegations an earlier Liverpool John Moores University investigation had not upheld. His latest accuser, Nathan Cofnas, had advanced ideas widely condemned as racist, making it impossible to regard his intervention as neutral. However, there was a clear public interest case for investigating such allegations. The Guardian sought to establish what was true. That is the proper function of journalism. Reporters were contacted by Arday over a year ago and worked extensively to verify what he had told them. In many instances they could not. It was right for the Guardian to publish its investigation, and it is wrong that the journalists who did their job responsibly are now being subjected to an onslaught of abuse. Cambridge, which has many of its own questions to answer, announced that it would hold an internal inquiry. In its journalism, the Guardian sought to meet tests of importance and proportionality, covering the issue with nuance. This could not be said of much of the rightwing media and its social media outriders. Arday became an exhibit in an ideological, almost Trumpian campaign against diversity and inclusion. The allegations were no longer simply about one academic’s behaviour or his past record. They were used to suggest that Arday had never deserved to be there – and that he had only been advanced because of his race. The attacks were relentless, often partisan, and amplified without respite online. This is racism at work. White academics are generally allowed to fail as individuals. Black ones are not. Arday may have had questions to answer; that did not make black academics collectively answerable for him. A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else: to be flawed, to make mistakes, and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race. title: The Guardian view on a vibrant summer for British athletics: inspiring a generation | Editorial
content: Amy Hunt’s record haul of four golds in Birmingham showcased the sport’s appeal. More can be done to ensure it gets its fair share of the limelight To win one gold medal is impressive. To win two indicates a certain relentlessness. To win four in the space of one remarkable week of athletics may ensure further recognition for Amy Hunt as the BBC’s sports personality of the year. Ms Hunt’s record‑breaking achievement in winning the 100m, 200m, women’s relay and mixed relay at the first European championships to be held in Britain was an exhibition of world-class sprinting for the ages. Her triumph capped a week which reminded us that there is more to sporting life than football. By winning an 11th medal, Dina Asher-Smith became the most successful athlete in the history of the competition. And on Friday, at a packed Alexander athletics stadium in Birmingham, the crowd savoured a contest and burgeoning rivalry that recalled the halcyon days of Sebastian Coe and Steve Ovett. Audrey Werro, the young Swiss star, and Keely Hodgkinson, Team GB’s Olympic champion, produced a thrillingly intense women’s 800m final, which Werro won with a time that broke a European record set in 1982. Athletics fans should relish the moment. The walls are closing in as another Premier League season begins, sucking the oxygen of publicity away from rival sports. An expanded World Cup, and the fallout from plans to sell a stake in the competition to private equity, made it seem as if football never went away. But it has been a stellar couple of months for British athletes. Josh Kerr’s shattering of the one-mile world record, in front of 60,000 spectators at July’s London Diamond League meet, was the sporting event of the summer until Hunt arguably trumped it. There was also a successful salvage operation in Scotland. Glasgow’s staging of the Commonwealth Games at short notice, after the original Australian hosts pulled out, rescued the event from limbo. The only downside was that the rich talent on display did not, at times, get the fanfare it deserved. Glasgow’s efforts went somewhat under the national radar after cost-conscious organisers rejected a low offer from the BBC and sold rights to the Discovery channel. The boost that terrestrial coverage can give was shown by an audience estimated to be in the region of 4 million for the epic runoff between Werro and Hodgkinson. Birmingham, however, has had its own problems as cameras panned across acres of empty seats in the early part of last week. The former athlete and BBC commentator Steve Cram has been among those to question high ticket prices, and there was a notable lack of cut-price deals to attract the next generation of athletics fans. The promotion and marketing of the event in Birmingham itself, in stark contrast with the 2022 Commonwealth Games, was somewhat underwhelming. For a sport which can produce such scintillating moments of concentrated drama, and in which male and female athletes enjoy a genuine equality of esteem, that is a shame. British athletics is enjoying a golden era, and sassy personalities such as Hunt – a Cambridge graduate who once described herself as “an ­academic badass and a track ­goddess” – have a charismatic appeal. The chosen motto of the London 2012 Olympics was “Inspire a generation”. As the likes of Hunt, Hodgkinson and Kerr do just that, more can be done to support and promote their efforts. Football may now be back. But Britain’s stars of track and field jumped through their annual summer window of opportunity to stunning effect.

title: The Guardian view on the changed world of job interviews: missing the human factor | Editorial
content: Andy Burnham’s doubts about Zoom interviews apply more widely to a hiring process being transformed by AI Almost half of UK jobseekers have found themselves pitching to an AI bot, according to recent research, leading many to give up in frustration. As one despairing applicant lamented in the pages of the Guardian a few months ago: “The hiring process has become so mechanised, both figuratively and literally, that it’s hard to believe that the people who end up getting hired aren’t merely the best at gaming the system.” For young people especially, experiencing repeated rejection without interacting with a single human being is alienating as well as disappointing. It was encouraging, therefore, to hear Andy Burnham voice concerns about online recruitment processes on a recent employment-focused podcast. Describing the jobseeking environment for young people as “harsh”, the prime minister criticised the widespread use of interviews on Zoom and Microsoft Teams, and questioned whether applicants could properly convey their personal qualities without a face-to-face meeting. There is another side to the story, as Zoom executives were swift to point out. Online interviewing cuts out travel costs, for example, giving a chance to applicants who may not be able to fund long journeys and possible overnight stays. But Mr Burnham is right to identify a dangerous drift towards selection processes that undervalue the worth of conversations between people in the same room at the same time. The increasingly used “one-way” video interview – in which applicants are given fixed periods of time to plan and deliver responses to prerecorded questions – seems to offer a particularly disorientating experience. Interviewees, in effect, speak into a void, unable to process feedback or interpret body language. The sorting processes deployed in AI interviews have been rightly criticised for their opacity, and susceptibility to algorithmic bias. A lack of transparency in relation to the programming of recruitment software means that an unlevel playing field may be suspected but difficult to prove. The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission settled an age discrimination case with a company that came to light only when a failed applicant reapplied, changing just her age, and miraculously passed through to the next round. It could hardly be claimed that traditional recruitment processes were bias-free. Used in the right way, new technologies can play their part in opening up possibilities for applicants rather than simply screening them out with minimal explanation or feedback. But while it may be convenient for businesses to rely on tech to do the work, the struggle even to present one’s credentials to another human being is adding insult to injuries already inflicted by an exceptionally unforgiving labour market. A recent report from the Institute for Public Policy Research found that young people in England were increasingly “losing faith in their futures”. The Information Commissioner’s Office has been tasked by parliament with producing a code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. In a recent report it found that when companies claimed that AI-generated hiring recommendations were subjected to human review, that was often only partially true, if at all. Applicants deserve better. The use of digital technologies is already changing the face of the entry-level jobs market. Interviewees should be protected from the downsides of their growing dominance in the recruitment process. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on London’s social housing: pumping billions into the economy every year | Editorial
content: The provision of homes needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded. It is vital economic infrastructure, so let’s make it affordable for all London’s city centre has long been a place where rich and poor live side by side, while so many other metropolitan equivalents – Paris, New York, San Francisco – remain the preserve of the rich. It maintains its mix today: in many inner London boroughs, between 20% and 40% of households live in social housing. A small but steady decline in social housing in these areas leaves many fearing that the city’s diversity is under threat. What happens when cities become less socially mixed? The G15 group of housing associations, which provide social and affordable homes for about one in 10 Londoners, commissioned research recently on the economic contribution of those living in social housing. It found that they contributed £27.8bn to London’s economy in 2024, even after housing benefit was taken into account. Its methodology involved comparing the lives of people in social housing with those without a stable and affordable place to live. The conclusion was that stable and affordable housing reduces spend and demand on public services, promotes better physical and mental overall health, and results in a higher likelihood that tenants stay in work and contribute economically. The idea that social housing is an economic investment is not new. England’s municipal housing was designed in recognition that a city could not function without healthy employees living nearby. Gordon Brown and Tony Blair revisited this idea in the early 2000s, arguing that England’s public services would deteriorate if hospital workers and police officers were pushed out of major urban centres. They framed social housing not as a charitable act, but as critical economic infrastructure. The G15 report finds that key workers such as nurses and care and retail workers account for about 65% of London’s social housing population (compared with 40% of London’s population). Not so long ago, these same workers were clapped in the streets for keeping cities functioning during the Covid-19 pandemic; they were the reason that people could buy milk and elderly people remained cared for while others had to stay at home. But many such workers would not be able to afford to live in big cities without the help of social housing. Even moving to the outer bounds of the city would add thousands to their commuting bill, as well as hours to their working days, according to the research. Viewed through that lens, housing that average-wage earners can afford becomes a vital asset for the country’s resilience. Social rents are proof that housing costs need not be a key driver of poverty – and yet our current building targets aren’t being pursued urgently enough to fix the problem. Housing charities say that 90,000 social homes a year are needed in England. No major party has plans for anything like that number. Mr Blair shifted social housing from councils towards housing associations, and the coalition commercialised that model. Andy Burnham now appears to want to put councils back at the centre. In an interview with the London Review of Books in 2024, Mr Burnham said: “If you read Nye Bevan’s speeches, as I do, if you read his speech that was the postwar Housing Act, second reading, he talked about how housing needs to be thought of as a service, not a commodity to be traded and sold, a wealth creator. Everybody needs it, it’s an essential service. And it was interesting how he positioned it like the NHS. And so that’s the philosophy that we need.” Amen to that. title: The Guardian view on Nigel Farage: Clacton cannot acquit him | Editorial
content: Reform won a contrived byelection, but scrutiny continues – while the party increasingly attacks the watchdogs and journalists asking awkward questions Nigel Farage didn’t attend the count of the byelection he forced upon Clacton. Instead, Reform UK’s leader celebrated his win with supporters at a “Farage Fest”, filmed by a friendly TV channel. For a politician who claims to speak for the people, it was telling that at his triumph he preferred an audience of believers. Mr Farage won because his toughest opponent on the campaign trail was a comedian in a jumpsuit with a bin on his head. That Count Binface nevertheless won 27% of the vote captured the absurdity of a contest the main parties had boycotted as a Faragist stunt. Reform UK’s leader wanted to turn scrutiny of his finances – notably an investigation into whether he failed to report a £5m gift from an overseas crypto billionaire – into a “fight” with the “establishment”. But the result determined who represents the Essex seat, not whether he broke parliamentary or electoral rules. There is no drop in enthusiasm among Mr Farage’s Clacton supporters. But he engineered an election in the safest territory – and despite facing no significant competition, had 37% vote against him. If even this part of the country can mobilise a substantial anti-Reform protest vote when the main parties stand aside, then imagine what might be possible in marginals where a mainstream challenger would prove more formidable. Mr Farage also hasn’t escaped the accountability he was trying to outrun. The parliamentary commissioner for standards suspended the investigation when he stopped being an MP; his re-election means the inquiry has resumed. It covers both the millions from the Thailand-based crypto magnate Christopher Harborne, and alleged undeclared support from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell. A mandate is not an acquittal. If the commissioner finds a serious breach of the rules and Mr Farage is suspended for 10 or more Commons sitting days, a recall petition in Clacton would follow. If 10% of electors signed it – roughly 1,500 fewer than voted for Count Binface – another byelection would be triggered. This time Mr Farage would face voters after parliamentary censure and a successful recall campaign, not just, as Labour claimed, reeking of the “stench of sleaze”. With the main parties likely to stand, the anti-Farage vote could also coalesce behind one serious challenger – and present a tougher test. A disturbing pattern is emerging around Reform’s intimidatory tactics. Questions about its funding are repeatedly answered not openly but by attacking those asking. A parliamentary watchdog becomes a “kangaroo court”; Reform deputy leader Richard Tice’s lawyers seek material that could identify sources behind the Guardian’s investigation; and a prominent Farage ally reportedly hired private investigators to examine a Sunday Times journalist investigating the party’s finances. This is likely to backfire for Reform. Last September the party was polling 32% nationally. After Mr Farage announced in July that he was triggering a byelection, it dropped from 27% to 24% – squeezed by a resurgent Labour, recovering Conservative party and Restore Britain’s more extreme policies. As even supporters such as Tim Montgomerie acknowledge, a political party built on voters’ grievances has now become increasingly preoccupied with its own grievances about the media, investigations and treatment of Mr Farage. The result is that Reform appears inward-looking, defensive and sleazy. That will probably damage the party more than its angry, divisive nationalism, which demonises minorities and shreds Britain’s traditions of tolerance and pluralism. title: The Guardian view on booming poetry sales: Homer, meet the Instapoets | Editorial
content: In an unexpected twist, a Hollywood epic has contributed to Britain’s best-ever half-year in poetry sales In a short story called Career Move, published in the New Yorker in 1992, Martin Amis imagined a world in which screenwriters wrote for little magazines and earned a pittance while poets were global superstars. Amis’s story, a wonderfully ironic inversion of the time-honoured norm, was surprisingly prescient: the film and TV industries have been struggling, with screenwriters facing contracting outlets for their creations, whereas poets are now big business. The Bookseller reported recently that poetry sales were at a historic high. Part of the increase can be attributed to Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey, which has made Homer hot: editions of The Odyssey and its prequel, The Iliad, have garnered almost £1m in book sales in the UK this year. (As well as valiantly trying to keep the ailing film industry afloat, Nolan has also created a craze for epic poetry.) But Nolan’s film does not solely account for the boom in poetry sales. Even without the Homer run, sales of poetry texts and anthologies were still up by 7.2% from what was historically already a very high base. The poets leading the charge are not the traditional behemoths – Berryman and the Brownings, Marvell and Milton, Pope and Pound. These remain acquired tastes, read (if at all) in the beleaguered bowers and tottering towers of organised “Eng lit”. The publishing sensations fuelling the poetic sales surge are “Instagram poets” such as Donna Ashworth, Rupi Kaur, Amanda Lovelace and Lucas Jones, whose collection, I Still Believe in Miracles, has netted £400,000 in sales this year. The appeal of this new generation lies in their directness. They want to be our new best friend. “Maybe you kinda feel how I feel,” says Jones in the introduction to I Still Believe in Miracles. The American poet Lovelace dedicates her 2022 collection, unlock your storybook heart (she eschews capital letters throughout), to “anyone who feels like they’ve yet to find themselves: i promise it’s not too late”. Lovelace advises readers to practise “self-care before, during and after reading”. Critics dismiss such work as more therapy than poetry, and argue it should be filed under self-help. Since the emergence of Instapoetry online in the middle of the last decade, a fault line has developed among poets as well as critics. Rebecca Watts’ dismissal in a 2018 article in PN Review, a poetry journal, of poets such as Kaur, Kae Tempest and Hollie McNish as “artless and amateur”, laid bare the divisions. The Instapoets have now successfully migrated to print, but the arguments continue. Is this literature for a post-literate age, or a healthy riposte to canonical poets (mostly “male, pale and stale” in the eyes of their detractors)? A corrective to the canon is no doubt overdue, and poets who appeal to a young readership beset by mental health issues should not be written off. But there are dangers. In June, Faber published Talking in Bed, a slim anthology of Philip Larkin poems in which there is a sense of Larkin being co-opted by the poetry-as-therapy movement. “He finds a way of admitting and delineating our nagging questions and most complicated feelings,” intones the blurb. The acerbic Larkin would not, one suspects, have appreciated this. Poetry should be allowed to be hermetic as well as accessible, and threatening as well as therapeutic. title: The Guardian view on Japan’s yen: Trump wants to keep the easy-money machine running | Editorial
content: A cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are useful Japan’s yen has slid back towards 160 to the dollar, despite last month’s extraordinary US-Japanese intervention. Traders are betting that its role as a cheap funding pipeline for global finance will continue. Earlier this month the Trump administration stepped in to help Tokyo stabilise its currency. “Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor,” Donald Trump explained. More help is likely to be on its way. But this is less a rescue of the yen than an attempt by Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, to preserve a cash spigot that benefits the US. Japan’s ultra-cheap money has become a global funding utility: bankers borrow yen, sell them for dollars and buy higher-returning US assets, notably tech shares. Rising American stock markets support collateral and investment. Japan’s “carry trade” is one of the reasons Wall Street can lever hundreds of billions into AI. Research suggests AI sucks up more than 1% of US GDP. Washington wants to keep this tap open, but not at the cost of a collapsing yen or US treasury sales. This column predicted this in April, warning that Tokyo’s monetary choices had bound US markets to the yen trade. What Mr Bessent did was to sell at least $10bn in euros and buy yen to arrest its slide to a 40-year low. Not telling the Europeans said it all: allies matter to Washington only when they are useful. Traders are probing US resolve. Rising oil prices, driven by US-Iran tensions, stoke Japan’s inflation and weaken the yen. Suppose it slides back to 164 yen to the dollar? Tokyo might respond with aggressive rate rises. This would be unlikely, as it would choke off the investment cycle that Japan is trying to create. It could also trigger a chaotic market unwind: higher rates shrink the gap between investors’ returns and yen borrowing; a stronger yen also makes yen‑denominated debts costlier to repay; investors then sell US assets to buy the yen needed to close their positions. That strengthens the yen further, inflicting bigger losses and forcing more US asset sales. A currency correction could quickly become a Wall Street rout. If Mr Bessent dislikes that option, he hates the alternative: Japan selling its $1.1tn treasury pile to buy yen. Dumping US debt would drive yields higher – and leave Washington with a costlier interest bill. Instead, Mr Bessent has allowed Japan to borrow dollars against its treasuries and use those dollars to buy yen. He has used a Federal Reserve lending facility to help – and wants its current $60bn daily limit substantially increased. This would give Tokyo room to stabilise the yen without having to choose between abandoning its reflationary programme and selling treasuries. If Mr Bessent gets his way, the Fed could turn a substantial portion of Japan’s trillion-dollar hoard of US government securities into cash. Argentina showed Mr Bessent would put American firepower behind currencies, spending billions to prop up the peso. Japan is the bigger challenge. He is asking traders: are you sure that you want to return to 164 yen to the dollar? He has form as a currency trader. Mr Bessent made George Soros a billion dollars in 1992 by selling pounds and forcing sterling from the European exchange rate mechanism. In 2013, Mr Bessent helped George Soros make another billion dollars betting against the Japanese currency. Margaret Thatcher famously said that “you can’t buck the market”. Mr Bessent is saying you can – as long you rewrite its rules. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone | Editorial
content: The response to this summer’s record heat and drought should be led by ministers – not left to the emergency services The wildfire that began on protected heathland in the New Forest in Hampshire on Sunday was reported to be under control on Tuesday. But with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or higher in parts of England on Thursday, the risk of further outbreaks remains high. Firefighters responded to 185 wildfires in the first 10 days of August. In coastal Suffolk, conservationists and locals are counting the cost of the blaze that devastated Dunwich Heath. Its vegetation and rare bird populations are expected to take decades to recover. Although the immediate cause of many wildfires is litter, the risks are elevated by heat and drought, and repeated warnings from climate scientists do not necessarily lessen the shock and distress caused. As people and governments across Europe assess this summer’s damage, experts including the UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, hope that the fires will focus minds on the urgent necessity of cutting emissions – as well as investing in emergency planning. Europe is currently heating up faster than any other continent, due in part to proximity to the melting Arctic. The global, existential nature of the climate crisis makes it an awkward fit with Andy Burnham’s current focus on “everyday fixes”. But if he does not find more to say about the summer’s disasters, he is in danger of being left behind. The National Trust has already surpassed its £500,000 fundraising target to restore Dunwich Heath. Conservationists and farmers are publicly debating the best ways to prevent fires. The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) is pushing for 5,000 additional firefighters across the UK, along with new equipment. In March, the then fire safety minister, Samantha Dixon, said that the fire and rescue service had suffered from “decades of drift and inertia”. Her speech also confirmed that a new College of Fire and Rescue would oversee professional standards, as recommended by the Grenfell inquiry. But three weeks ago Ms Dixon was sacked. If the government wants to avoid an impression that drift and inertia are ongoing, they need to provide an update, along with a response to repeated calls from the fire service inspectorate for new enforcement powers. MPs on the home affairs committee threw their weight behind this idea two years ago. The fire and rescue service is popular with the public. Even highly critical sections of the Grenfell inquiry report did not significantly undermine confidence in it. This summer’s events seem likely to reaffirm this positive regard, and rightly so: public servants who do dangerous, difficult jobs, when many other people are on holiday, deserve to be appreciated. But scrutiny of the service is also important. An inquiry by the home affairs select committee, which was summarised in a letter to the home secretary in 2024, contained strong criticism of its culture and leadership. Such concerns deserve a fuller response than they have so far received from ministers. So do the FBU’s call for investment to cope with rising risks, and proposals for a temporary ban on disposable barbecues. Ill-informed and ideological attempts to blame rewilding should also be addressed by ministers. Working groups on how to reduce wildfire risks must produce plans. The latest report from the government’s Climate Change Committee found that existing adaptation plans are not fit for purpose. This summer’s extraordinary heat, drought and wildfires should be a spur to action on both the fire service and the wider climate crisis.
centralIdea: The escalating wildfire crisis in the UK, driven by climate change, cannot be managed by emergency services alone; it requires urgent ministerial leadership, policy updates, and robust climate adaptation plans.

title: The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | Editorial
content: Amid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome development As the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writing thinkpieces on what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this week published 6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future. Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of his essay – which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity. Replicating a strategy deployed by cryptocurrency backers in the 2024 election cycle, Silicon Valley is pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Super Pacs – groups unaffiliated to political parties or campaigns – to ensure that voices sympathetic to its deregulatory AI agenda get elected. OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, and Palantir’s co-founder, Jo Lonsdale, have given large sums to Leading the Future, an organisation dedicated to “identifying, maintaining, and growing pro-AI candidates”. Vast amounts are being spent to try to tilt the balance in individual contests, sometimes through disingenuous means. Earlier this summer, Leading the Future spent $6m on ads attacking Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and pioneer of AI regulation at state level. Rather than focus on his AI campaigning, the ads attacked Mr Bores’s progressive credentials, alleging that he had carried out tech work in the past for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he denies. Running for Congress in a Democratic stronghold, he lost a tight primary race after battling what was in essence a smear campaign. Countervailing forces are emerging. Guardrails Alliance, a union-backed Super Pac, is attempting to combat Leading the Future’s influence, while a bipartisan groundswell of opposition to datacentres is generating serious electoral clout. But as tech companies and their billionaire owners seek to shape and above all limit the scope of AI regulation, their influence is distorting debate in a political culture where the power of money already holds far too much sway. In his essay, Mr Zuckerberg urges that AI’s democratising potential be protected from those who believe “a small set of experts … should decide what is best for humanity”. He appears to miss the irony that an unelected tech oligarchy, to which he belongs, is already performing that function by default. Its pressure has been instrumental in persuading Donald Trump to cancel the signing of an executive order which would have given the government the right to review new AI models. Its wealth is now being used to attack and undermine dissenting voices in the public square. If a democratic debate about the benefits and dangers of AI is to take place, such presumption must be fiercely resisted in the US and elsewhere. The semi-covert manipulation of political discussion is no way to map out an inclusive future in challenging times.

title: The Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in Jerusalem | Editorial
content: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted At the end of July, Donald Trump announced that a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it was reported that another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe. Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitly rejected the sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.” In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazen violation of the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle. Formal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largely destroyed and the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first building contract issued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted  to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievous miscalculation in which Israel’s prime minister also played his part. In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue a scorched earth project of revenge following the Hamas massacre of October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruption charges first laid more than five years ago. Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point. Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recent polling suggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza. title: The Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front foot | Editorial
content: Privacy needs defending against invasive wearable gadgets. So far, businesses are ahead of the government It is not yet clear to what extent Meta’s new smart glasses will live up to the nickname of “pervert glasses” – bestowed in recognition of the obvious appeal of wearable cameras to voyeurs. The past week has seen rising criticism of the devices, which in the UK have been banned by the pub chain Wetherspoons and the theatre group ATG, as well as restaurants, schools and members’ clubs. These organisations deserve praise for standing up for privacy. By contrast, regulators appear once again to be on the back foot. There have, inevitably, already been reports of women being mistreated. Earlier this year the BBC spoke to several who had been filmed without their consent, with footage subsequently uploaded to social media. In one case, the content creator demanded a fee to remove it. In the year to March 2025, image-based sexual abuse and cyberflashing were responsible for more than half of an 11% increase in reported sexual offences in England and Wales. Normalisation of smart glasses would, clearly, make such offences easier to commit. Worrying as this is, it is not the only reason to be concerned. Privacy has much wider significance and most people, as the businesses banning smart glasses from their premises have recognised, do not want to be filmed as they go about their lives. While videoing in public is not illegal, this does not give smart glasses wearers the right to place others under involuntary surveillance. An LED light that blinks when the camera is in use, and cannot be disabled, is not an adequate safeguard, whatever Meta might think. Pubs, parks, beaches and workplaces are not film sets. Having invested $80bn in its latest product, Mark Zuckerberg’s company is unlikely to give up easily on its ambition to make the glasses, which have been likened to face-mounted smartphones, as ubiquitous as the handheld kind. More than a decade after the first smart glasses, made by Google, flopped, Meta has bet heavily on making its latest version more stylish, functional and affordable – with UK prices starting at £269. The choice of Kylie Jenner to front this summer’s advertising campaign, and the slogan “Never miss a moment”, aimed at parents of young children, appear calculated to dispel fears about how the glasses will be used by sexually predatory men. Like most digital devices, these ones can be helpful as well as harmful. As aids for people who are blind or visually impaired, smart glasses that can read text or describe images have been described as life-changing. Any restrictions, in the UK or elsewhere, should be crafted so as to enable such uses to continue – just as guide dogs are exempted from rules about pets. But while the benefits that smart glasses offer to groups of people with specific needs should be recognised, this must not be allowed to distract from their potential to cause harm. Tech regulation is difficult. But given the UK government’s recent moves towards restricting smartphone use among young people, and the public outcry regarding sexualised AI imagery, it is disappointing that ministers have so far had almost nothing to say about the rollout of wearable hidden cameras. While the tech companies market their products as tools to be used, one of the key lessons of the last two decades is that users are rarely, if ever, as in control as they would like to be. Ministers and regulators should be active, not passive, as Meta intentionally blurs the line between looking and filming. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the two cultures: bridge the divide, starting with A-levels | Editorial
content: Seventy years after CP Snow warned of estrangement between the sciences and arts, breadth in education should be encouraged After the playwright Tom Stoppard died last year, one of the most striking tributes to his work came from a clinical scientist. Michael Baum explained in the British Medical Journal how, in the interval of a 1993 performance of Arcadia, he experienced an epiphany. Thomasina Coverly’s attempt to plot the equation for a rose prompted him to realise that chaos theory was the best way to explain breast cancer’s pattern of recurrence. It was, he wrote, “the bond that links the arts and the sciences as one enterprise rather than the contents of two silos”. Mr Baum was not the first person to celebrate the bridging of this gap. CP Snow famously criticised the incuriosity of “literary intellectuals” about technology in his essay The Two Cultures (later turned into a lecture and a book). Whether or not this was justified at the time, many literary intellectuals besides Stoppard have since taken a close interest in science; Richard Holmes’s latest book, about the influence of evolutionary theory on Tennyson, is just one example. But the split between the humanities and sciences remains pronounced, and will be evident when this year’s A-level results are released on Thursday. Stoppard’s Thomasina was talking to her maths tutor when she sparked Mr Baum’s chain of associations. For anyone interested in linking disciplines, education is clearly crucial. But while recent decades have seen successful efforts to boost Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics), at the expense of the humanities and arts, the division between these two broad fields of knowledge has been unaddressed. So has the issue of early specialisation, with many pupils in England and Wales choosing either one path or the other at age 16. This narrowing is highly unusual internationally. In France, Germany, the US and Scotland, pupils typically study a broader curriculum until they leave school. And while theoretically, English and Welsh teenagers at least have a wide choice of subjects, and there is nothing to stop them from studying chemistry alongside dance or German, timetables can make this difficult, while the competitive nature of university admissions incentivises them to stick to what they are best at, whether that is a suite of essay-writing subjects or physics, maths and further maths. This tendency to specialise has intensified recently. Under New Labour, pupils were encouraged to take four subjects in year 12 before choosing three A-levels. But following Michael Gove’s decision to scrap AS assessments, the options narrowed both in terms of the number of subjects studied and the range. Between 2003 and 2021, the proportion of students taking A-levels from a single subject-group rose from 18% to 35%. Only 5% of the latter cohort studied a combination of Stem, social science and humanities subjects. Last year the government cut funding for state schools teaching the wide‑ranging international baccalaureate. There is no shortage of challenges facing the new education secretary, Lucy Powell – not least the repeatedly botched reform of vocational alternatives, and the rise in pupils with special educational needs. That’s one reason why A-levels barely featured in the recent curriculum review. But the 70th anniversary of Snow’s “two cultures” thesis is a good time to reflect on whether a rethink of 16-to-18 education is due. Young people should be enabled to keep more options open for longer. More people straddling the science and humanities disciplines would be a good thing.
